Abstract

This project examines job satisfaction among employed people in Switzerland using 21 annual waves of the Swiss Household Panel (2004–2024). The employed sample contains 124,769 respondent-year observations. We investigate occupational and demographic differences, changes around the 2009 financial crisis, the 2015 Swiss franc shock and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, and whether occupational gaps vary across broader economic periods. Exploratory analysis and preliminary OLS regressions with respondent-clustered standard errors show that satisfaction differs across groups and years. The unweighted annual mean declined from 8.212 in 2004 to 7.815 in 2024, and occupation-by-period interactions are jointly significant. The results describe associations, not causal effects, and are subject to missingness, changing sample composition and survey-design limitations.

1 Introduction

1.1 Project Goals

Job satisfaction is an important topic in management and organisational behaviour because it is connected to employees’ experiences at work and to decisions about retention and working conditions. However, satisfaction is shaped by several factors, including the type of work, employment arrangements, career opportunities and the wider economic environment. Looking only at one company or one point in time may therefore provide a limited picture.

This project examines job satisfaction among employed people in Switzerland using the Swiss Household Panel (SHP). By combining annual survey data from 2004 to 2024, we aim to understand how satisfaction differs between occupational and demographic groups, how it has evolved over time, and whether the differences between occupations vary across economic periods. Switzerland provides a useful setting because its labour market includes different occupations and regions and experienced several major economic events during the study period, notably the 2009 financial crisis, the 2015 Swiss franc shock and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic.

Our objective is to describe patterns in job satisfaction and test whether observed differences are statistically significant. The project follows a data science workflow: preparing and harmonising multiple survey waves, exploring distributions and trends, comparing groups, and applying statistical models. The findings may help inform discussions about employee well-being and workforce management, but the analysis identifies associations rather than causal effects.

Compared with our initial proposal, we refined the analysis to 2004–2024, because the general job satisfaction measure was unavailable in several earlier waves. We also clarified that the regional variable refers to region of residence, not workplace location. Employment arrangements are included as an additional dimension of group comparisons. Since some respondents appear in multiple years, our preliminary regressions use standard errors clustered by respondent rather than treating every respondent-year observation as independent.

1.2 Research Questions

Main research question: How does job satisfaction in Switzerland vary across occupational groups, age, gender and region, and how does it evolve during periods of economic stress?

  • RQ1.1: What are the differences in average job satisfaction between occupational groups, age groups, men and women, and regions? We also examine differences by employment arrangement.
  • RQ1.2: How does job satisfaction change around major economic events (the 2009 financial crisis, the 2015 Swiss franc shock and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic) compared with surrounding years and, where feasible, calmer periods?
  • RQ1.3: How do differences in job satisfaction between occupational groups change across different economic periods?

RQ1.1 focuses on differences between groups of workers. RQ1.2 examines changes around specific events, using comparisons of the year before, the event year and the following year. RQ1.3 considers whether occupational gaps remain similar across four broader periods: 2004–2008, 2009–2014, 2015–2019 and 2020–2024.

1.3 Related Work

Job satisfaction is commonly studied through employee surveys, but a national household panel offers a broader perspective than a survey conducted within one organisation. The SHP follows respondents across survey waves and provides information on job satisfaction alongside occupational and demographic characteristics (SHP Group, 2026). This allows us to examine differences across groups and years using a consistent survey source.

For data preparation, we use pandas to clean, harmonise and merge annual files, following standard Python data-analysis practices described by McKinney (2022) and the pandas documentation (pandas development team, n.d.). We use Matplotlib for exploratory figures (Matplotlib development team, n.d.). Our preliminary analysis then uses descriptive statistics and ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to test group differences and changes across economic periods, implemented with statsmodels (statsmodels developers, n.d.). Respondent-clustered standard errors account for correlation between repeated observations of the same person. These methods are appropriate for an initial assessment of associations, but they do not fully address survey design, changing sample composition or unobserved differences between respondents. We discuss these limitations when interpreting the results.

The SHP dataset is managed by FORS and distributed through SWISSUbase. We use Version 12.0, but exclude the beta Wave 27 and analyse only the 2004–2024 waves (SHP Group, 2026). These references document the dataset and tools used; they are not presented as a systematic review of job-satisfaction research.

2 Data

2.1 Sources

Our primary data source is the Swiss Household Panel (SHP), Living in Switzerland Waves 1–26 + Long file + Beta version Wave 27, Version 12.0, published by FORS and distributed through SWISSUbase (SHP Group, 2026). The version-specific dataset DOI is 10.48573/haxy-c230; the canonical DOI is 10.48573/pjmf-8s41. Access for this educational research project was approved on 19 October 2026. We used the SAS files from the release, excluding the beta Wave 27.

Although the release contains waves dating back to 1999, our analysis covers 2004–2024 (21 annual waves) because the general job-satisfaction measure is unavailable in several earlier years. We combined annual individual and household records to study employed respondents across Switzerland. The underlying microdata are access-controlled; we do not redistribute them with the report.

2.2 Description

Our preparation process produced three related datasets:

Dataset Respondent-year observations Unique respondents Purpose
Full dataset 305,462 45,632 Harmonised individual and household records
Employed sample 124,769 22,265 Employed respondents with valid occupation and job satisfaction
Analysis sample 124,766 — Employed sample excluding missing age or sex

The full dataset has 10 standardised variables: IDPERS (respondent identifier), IDHOUS (household identifier), YEAR, AGE, SEX, EMPLOYMENT_STATUS, WORKING_STATUS, OCCUPATION, JOB_SATISFACTION and REGION. Job satisfaction is measured on a 0–10 scale; occupation is grouped using ISCO major groups; REGION describes region of residence, not necessarily the region of employment. Employment arrangements are analysed separately from the employment-status filter.

Each row represents a respondent in a particular survey year. Since individuals can appear in multiple waves, the number of rows is larger than the number of distinct respondents. The sample also varies across years and occupational groups, which matters when comparing means.

2.3 Loading Data

We initially read annual SAS files using Python and pyreadstat, selected the relevant columns and merged individual and household information. We then saved the harmonised datasets as CSV files under data/processed/, so the report can use the prepared data without rerunning the entire raw-data pipeline (McKinney, 2022; pandas development team, n.d.).

The following chunk loads the processed files using paths relative to the project root. It requires the three CSV files exported by 01_data_preparation.ipynb to be present in data/processed/.

2.4 Wrangling

2.4.1 General Transformations

We first inspected the available variables and their coding in the annual SHP files, testing the preparation procedure on individual waves before automating it for 2004–2024. For each wave, we selected the relevant individual and household variables, converted invalid survey codes to missing values, harmonised column names, merged the files using their appropriate identifiers and added the survey year. The annual datasets were then concatenated into a single dataset.

For the employed sample, we retained respondents with WORKING_STATUS == 1, a valid occupation code (ISCO major groups 0–9) and a job-satisfaction score from 0 to 10. We did not use EMPLOYMENT_STATUS as the employment filter: that variable is retained for comparisons of employment arrangements. The smaller analysis sample additionally excludes the two missing age values and one missing sex value in the employed sample. For some regressions, further complete-case restrictions apply; their sample sizes are reported in the Analysis section.

2.4.2 Spotting Mistakes and Missing Data

We checked identifiers, survey-year coverage, duplicates and missing values after combining the annual files. The full dataset contains no duplicate respondent-year combinations, and respondent ID, survey year, household ID and region are complete.

Variable Missing observations in full dataset
Age 232
Sex 4
Employment status 1,003
Occupation 180,252
Job satisfaction 178,161

The high missingness in occupation and job satisfaction partly reflects the inclusion of non-employed respondents in the full dataset. Rather than imputing these central research variables, we restrict the employed sample to observations with valid occupation and job-satisfaction values. This ensures the outcomes and occupational categories being compared are observed, although exclusions may affect representativeness.

2.4.3 Listing Anomalies and Outliers

We checked the survey’s special missing-value codes and the permitted ranges of key variables. Valid job-satisfaction scores from 0 to 10 were retained, including low and high responses; these are meaningful values rather than outliers to remove. The Armed Forces occupation group (ISCO 0) is present but small (131 observations in the demographic analysis sample), so it is excluded from the civilian-occupation regressions and some comparative figures. We also checked for duplicate respondent-year records and found none.

2.4.4 Survey Weights and Comparability

The SHP provides annual individual cross-sectional survey weights for all 21 analysed years. We matched these to the employed sample by respondent ID and year. 121,547 of 124,769 observations (97.42%) have positive weights; 3,222 have zero or negative weight codes and were excluded from weighted calculations.

Annual mean job satisfaction 2004 2024 Change
Unweighted 8.212 7.815 −0.397
Weighted 8.207 7.711 −0.496

Both comparisons indicate a decline over the period. We retain unweighted results for the main exploratory analysis and use weighted annual means as a robustness comparison. The weights were not adjusted specifically for the employed subgroup, and these calculations do not implement the full complex survey design. Similarly, repeated observations of the same respondents require care in formal statistical testing; the preliminary regressions use respondent-clustered standard errors.

The complete data preparation and validation code is retained in 01_data_preparation.ipynb; this update report presents the essential decisions and checks rather than reproducing every processing step.

3 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

We examine the distribution of job satisfaction, its development from 2004 to 2024, and differences across occupations, demographic groups, employment arrangements and economic periods. All figures use unweighted respondent-year observations from the employed sample unless otherwise stated. Because respondents can appear in several years, these plots describe the sample rather than independent individuals. Statistical tests are discussed separately in the Analysis section.

3.1 Univariate Analysis

3.1.1 Distribution of job satisfaction

Code 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from IPython.display import display

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
scores = employed_sample["JOB_SATISFACTION"].dropna()
ax.hist(scores, bins=np.arange(-0.5, 11.5, 1), edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(scores.mean(), linestyle="--", color="black", label=f"Mean: {scores.mean():.2f}")
ax.set(xlabel="Job satisfaction (0–10)", ylabel="Respondent-year observations", xticks=range(11))
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

As shown in Figure 1, job satisfaction is concentrated toward the upper end of the 0–10 scale, with a median of 8. The distribution is not symmetric: relatively few respondents report very low satisfaction. For this reason, we examine both the mean and the percentage reporting low satisfaction (0–5) rather than relying on the mean alone.

3.1.2 Summary statistics and potential outliers

Code 
summary_stats = analysis_sample[["JOB_SATISFACTION", "AGE"]].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "std", "median", "min", "max"]
).T.rename(columns={"count": "N", "mean": "Mean", "std": "SD", "median": "Median", "min": "Minimum", "max": "Maximum"})
display(summary_stats.round(2))
Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.3))
sns.boxplot(x=scores, ax=ax, color="lightsteelblue")
ax.set(xlabel="Job satisfaction (0–10)", xlim=(-0.5, 10.5), xticks=range(11))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Table 1 reports the central tendency and spread of the two continuous variables used in the project. The distribution in Figure 2 is bounded by the questionnaire’s 0–10 scale and is concentrated toward high satisfaction. Values at the low end can appear as statistical outliers in a box plot, but they are valid survey responses, not data errors, so we do not remove them. The bounded, uneven distribution also motivates reporting medians and the low-satisfaction share alongside means. The subsequent regressions use respondent-clustered standard errors because individuals can contribute several observations.

3.2 Bivariate Analysis

3.2.1 Overall trend in job satisfaction

Code 
annual = (employed_sample.assign(LOW_SAT=employed_sample["JOB_SATISFACTION"].le(5))
          .groupby("YEAR", as_index=False)
          .agg(mean_satisfaction=("JOB_SATISFACTION", "mean"),
               low_satisfaction=("LOW_SAT", "mean")))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.plot(annual["YEAR"], annual["mean_satisfaction"], marker="o", markersize=3)
ax.set(xlabel="Survey year", ylabel="Mean satisfaction (0–10)")
ax.set_xticks([2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
display(annual.loc[annual["YEAR"].isin([2004, 2024])].round(3))

As shown in Figure 3, the unweighted mean fell from 8.212 in 2004 to 7.815 in 2024, a decline of 0.397 points. The percentage reporting low satisfaction rose from 6.27% to 7.56%. These are descriptive trends and may partly reflect changes in the respondents included each year.

3.2.2 Occupational differences (RQ1.1)

Code 
occupation_labels = {
    1: "Managers", 2: "Professionals", 3: "Technicians", 4: "Clerical support",
    5: "Service and sales", 6: "Agricultural", 7: "Craft workers",
    8: "Machine operators", 9: "Elementary occupations"
}
occ = employed_sample.loc[employed_sample["OCCUPATION"].isin(occupation_labels)].copy()
occ["Occupation"] = occ["OCCUPATION"].map(occupation_labels)
occ_summary = (occ.groupby("Occupation")["JOB_SATISFACTION"]
               .agg(["mean", "count"]).sort_values("mean"))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.barh(occ_summary.index, occ_summary["mean"])
ax.set(xlabel="Mean satisfaction (0–10)", ylabel="")
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

As shown in Figure 4, average satisfaction differs across occupational groups. Agricultural workers have the highest pooled average, while clerical support workers have the lowest among the nine civilian groups. We exclude Armed Forces (ISCO 0) from this comparison because of its small sample. Differences in occupation may overlap with age, region and employment arrangements; the Analysis section tests adjusted associations.

Age group

The group summaries in Table 2 show that satisfaction generally increases in older age groups, although these are comparisons across respondents, not evidence that aging causes higher satisfaction. Women report a slightly higher pooled mean than men. Very short part-time work and family-business work show higher unadjusted averages than full-time work, but their sample sizes are much smaller. The employment-arrangement comparison includes only records with the relevant valid categories. Region is region of residence, not necessarily workplace location. The regional descriptive comparison is shown next, with adjusted associations reported in the Analysis section.

Figure 5 compares the seven regions of residence, not workplace locations. The pooled averages show geographic variation in job satisfaction, which could partly reflect differences in workforce composition and employment conditions. This motivates including region as a covariate in the adjusted RQ1.1 model rather than interpreting these descriptive differences as regional effects.

3.2.5 Changes around economic events (RQ1.2)

Code 
event_years = {"2009 financial crisis": 2009, "2015 Swiss franc shock": 2015, "2020 COVID-19": 2020}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, (event, year) in zip(axes, event_years.items()):
    window = annual[annual["YEAR"].between(year - 1, year + 1)]
    ax.plot(window["YEAR"], window["mean_satisfaction"], marker="o")
    ax.set_title(event)
    ax.set_xticks([year - 1, year, year + 1])
    ax.set_xlabel("Year")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Mean satisfaction (0–10)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

As shown in Figure 6, the 2009 window shows a small decline; the 2015 window shows lower satisfaction during and after the franc shock; and 2020 shows a temporary increase followed by a return near the 2019 level in 2021. These windows are not causal estimates of the economic events. Respondent-clustered comparisons of the same years appear in the Analysis section.

3.3 Multivariate Analysis

3.3.1 Occupation across economic periods (RQ1.3)

Code 
period_data = occ.copy()
period_data["Economic period"] = pd.cut(
    period_data["YEAR"], bins=[2003, 2008, 2014, 2019, 2024],
    labels=["2004–2008", "2009–2014", "2015–2019", "2020–2024"]
)
period_means = period_data.pivot_table(
    index="Occupation", columns="Economic period", values="JOB_SATISFACTION",
    aggfunc="mean", observed=True
).reindex(list(occupation_labels.values()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.heatmap(period_means, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="YlGnBu", ax=ax,
            cbar_kws={"label": "Mean satisfaction"})
ax.set(xlabel="Economic period", ylabel="")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

As shown in Figure 7, occupational averages vary across the four broad periods, and the gaps between occupations are not identical in each period. These period labels are descriptive groupings, not four separate crisis treatments. The interaction regression in the Analysis section tests whether occupational differences vary significantly across periods.

3.4 Correlation Analysis and Choice of Visualisations

A conventional correlation matrix across the categorical variables would be misleading: OCCUPATION, SEX, REGION, and EMPLOYMENT_STATUS are numeric codes for categories, not continuous measurements. A correlation between their numeric codes would depend on the arbitrary numbering of categories. We therefore use group means, grouped comparisons, and the occupation-by-period heatmap instead of an inappropriate correlation heatmap or scatter plot. Relationships involving the continuous variable AGE are explored through age groups, which also makes the results easier to interpret for RQ1.1.

3.5 EDA Summary and Implications for Analysis

The figures and tables above indicate a gradual decline in overall satisfaction, differences across occupations and demographic groups, and distinct patterns around the three event windows. The weighted annual-mean check also indicates a decline from 2004 to 2024 (8.207 to 7.711), although the report’s main EDA remains unweighted. These findings motivate three sets of respondent-clustered regressions: adjusted group comparisons (RQ1.1), before/during/after event-window comparisons (RQ1.2), and an occupation-by-economic-period interaction (RQ1.3). The EDA supports the selection of occupation, age, sex, region, employment arrangement and survey year for RQ1.1; short event windows for RQ1.2; and occupation-by-period interaction terms for RQ1.3. The models and significance tests are presented in the Analysis section. None of these observational comparisons establishes causation.

4 Preliminary Analysis

4.1 Methods and rationale

We use ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to test whether the descriptive differences in job satisfaction are statistically distinguishable from zero. The outcome is the reported 0–10 job-satisfaction score. OLS gives coefficients in satisfaction points, which are straightforward to interpret; it is a practical first approach rather than a claim that the bounded outcome is normally distributed. We treat occupation, age groups, sex, region of residence, employment arrangement, survey year and economic periods as categorical variables where appropriate.

Respondents may appear in multiple waves, so standard errors are clustered by respondent (IDPERS) in every regression. This accounts for within-person correlation in standard errors, but does not eliminate confounding or fully incorporate the complex survey design. Models are unweighted; the separate survey-weight check is discussed in the Data section. All results are observational, not causal.

4.1.1 Model assumptions and checks

OLS assumes that the conditional mean is adequately specified, that the predictors are not perfectly collinear, and that errors are appropriately handled for inference. Normality of the job-satisfaction scores themselves is not an OLS requirement; however, the bounded, discrete 0–10 outcome and possible ceiling effects mean a linear model is an approximation. We have not formally verified residual normality, functional form or all other diagnostics, so we cannot claim that every assumption is satisfied. Coefficients should therefore be read as preliminary differences in mean satisfaction, not as precise causal effects.

The SHP follows individuals over time, so respondent-year observations are not independent. Clustering standard errors by IDPERS allows errors for the same respondent to be correlated across waves, but does not correct omitted-variable bias or changes in sample composition. The models use category indicators rather than treating occupation, sex or region codes as continuous quantities. The models also do not fully account for the SHP’s survey sampling design; a weighted sensitivity check for descriptive trends is reported in the Data section, not as validation of these regressions. We will consider model diagnostics, survey-design sensitivity checks and within-person specifications in the final report.

The three tests address different questions: (1) occupational and demographic differences after adjustment; (2) changes between the year before, during and after selected events; and (3) whether occupational gaps vary across four broader periods. Joint Wald tests evaluate whole groups of coefficients, rather than relying on isolated comparisons.

4.2 RQ1.1 — Occupation, demographics and employment arrangements

First, we compare nine civilian occupational groups while controlling for survey year. Armed Forces (occupation code 0) is excluded because of its very small sample. Clerical support workers (code 4) are the reference occupation.

Code 
rq11_data = analysis_sample[["IDPERS", "YEAR", "OCCUPATION", "JOB_SATISFACTION"]].dropna().copy()
rq11_data["OCCUPATION"] = pd.to_numeric(rq11_data["OCCUPATION"], errors="coerce")
rq11_data = rq11_data[rq11_data["OCCUPATION"].isin(range(1, 10))].copy()
rq11_data["OCCUPATION"] = rq11_data["OCCUPATION"].astype(int)
model_rq11 = smf.ols(
    "JOB_SATISFACTION ~ C(OCCUPATION, Treatment(reference=4)) + C(YEAR)",
    data=rq11_data
).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": rq11_data["IDPERS"]})
occ_terms = [t for t in model_rq11.params.index if t.startswith("C(OCCUPATION")]
occ_test = model_rq11.wald_test(" = 0, ".join(occ_terms) + " = 0", scalar=True)
selected = {1: "Managers", 2: "Professionals", 6: "Agricultural workers"}
rows = []
for code, name in selected.items():
    term = next(t for t in occ_terms if f"[T.{code}]" in t)
    rows.append({"Occupation": name, "Difference (points)": model_rq11.params[term], "p-value": model_rq11.pvalues[term]})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4))
print(f"N = {len(rq11_data):,}; respondent-clustered Wald chi-square({len(occ_terms)}) = {float(occ_test.statistic):.2f}; p = {float(occ_test.pvalue):.3g}; R² = {model_rq11.rsquared:.3f}")
N = 124,635; respondent-clustered Wald chi-square(8) = 168.22; p = 3.04e-32; R² = 0.010

As shown in Table 3, occupational differences are jointly significant (χ²(8) = 168.22, p < 0.001; 124,635 observations). Relative to clerical support workers, agricultural workers (+0.560 points), managers (+0.317) and professionals (+0.231) have higher average satisfaction after controlling for survey year. This is evidence of differences between occupational groups, not evidence that occupation itself causes satisfaction.

We then include age group, sex, region of residence and employment arrangement together with occupation and survey year. The sample is smaller because employment-arrangement categories must be valid; sex is restricted to codes 1 and 2. Age under 25, managers, sex code 1, region code 1 and full-time employment are the model’s reference categories.

Code 
rq11_full = analysis_sample[["IDPERS", "YEAR", "JOB_SATISFACTION", "OCCUPATION", "AGE", "SEX", "REGION", "EMPLOYMENT_STATUS"]].copy()
rq11_full = rq11_full[
    rq11_full["OCCUPATION"].isin(range(1, 10))
    & rq11_full["EMPLOYMENT_STATUS"].isin([1, 2, 3, 5])
    & rq11_full["SEX"].isin([1, 2])
].dropna().copy()
rq11_full["AGE_GROUP"] = pd.cut(
    rq11_full["AGE"], bins=[0, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, np.inf],
    labels=["Under 25", "25–34", "35–44", "45–54", "55–64", "65+"], include_lowest=True
)
model_rq11_full = smf.ols(
    "JOB_SATISFACTION ~ C(OCCUPATION) + C(AGE_GROUP) + C(SEX) + C(REGION) + C(EMPLOYMENT_STATUS) + C(YEAR)",
    data=rq11_full
).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": rq11_full["IDPERS"]})
joint_rows = []
for variable, label in [("OCCUPATION", "Occupation"), ("AGE_GROUP", "Age group"), ("SEX", "Sex"), ("REGION", "Region of residence"), ("EMPLOYMENT_STATUS", "Employment arrangement")]:
    terms = [t for t in model_rq11_full.params.index if t.startswith(f"C({variable})[")]
    test = model_rq11_full.wald_test(" = 0, ".join(terms) + " = 0", scalar=True)
    joint_rows.append({"Variable": label, "df": len(terms), "Wald χ²": float(test.statistic), "p-value": float(test.pvalue)})
display(pd.DataFrame(joint_rows).round(4))
print(f"N = {len(rq11_full):,}; respondents = {rq11_full['IDPERS'].nunique():,}; R² = {model_rq11_full.rsquared:.3f}")
N = 104,526; respondents = 18,363; R² = 0.039

As shown in Table 4, all five groups of predictors are jointly significant (each p < 0.001; 104,526 observations, 18,363 respondents, R² = 0.039). For example, clerical support workers score 0.321 points lower than managers, controlling for the included characteristics; respondents aged 65+ score 1.088 points higher than those under 25. Part-time employment of 5–36 hours differs only slightly from full-time work (−0.065 points). These comparisons do not imply that every category within a variable differs significantly. We retain numeric sex codes in model interpretation until their official labels are verified.

4.3 RQ1.2 — Changes around economic events

We estimate three separate event-window regressions comparing the year before each event with the event year and the following year: 2008–2010, 2014–2016 and 2019–2021. Each model uses respondent-clustered standard errors. These are year-to-year comparisons, not causal estimates of the events’ effects; they do not adjust for other changes occurring at the same time.

Code 
events = {"2009 Financial Crisis": 2009, "2015 Swiss Franc Shock": 2015, "2020 COVID-19": 2020}
event_rows = []
for event_name, event_year in events.items():
    subset = analysis_sample.loc[
        analysis_sample["YEAR"].isin([event_year - 1, event_year, event_year + 1]),
        ["IDPERS", "YEAR", "JOB_SATISFACTION"]
    ].dropna().copy()
    subset["PERIOD"] = pd.Categorical(
        subset["YEAR"].map({event_year - 1: "Before", event_year: "During", event_year + 1: "After"}),
        categories=["Before", "During", "After"]
    )
    fitted = smf.ols("JOB_SATISFACTION ~ C(PERIOD, Treatment(reference='Before'))", data=subset).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": subset["IDPERS"]}
    )
    for period in ["During", "After"]:
        term = next(t for t in fitted.params.index if f"[T.{period}]" in t)
        event_rows.append({"Event": event_name, "Comparison": f"{period} vs before", "Difference (points)": fitted.params[term], "p-value": fitted.pvalues[term], "N": len(subset)})
display(pd.DataFrame(event_rows).round(4))

As shown in Table 5, the 2009 event-year change is not significant (−0.034, p = 0.147), while 2010 is slightly lower than 2008 (−0.053, p = 0.026). The 2015 and 2016 comparisons are both negative and significant (−0.068 and −0.089, respectively; both p < 0.001). In 2020, satisfaction is temporarily higher than in 2019 (+0.078, p < 0.001), but the 2021 difference is effectively zero (+0.001, p = 0.977). The magnitudes are small, and the 2009 after-year result warrants particular caution given multiple comparisons.

4.4 RQ1.3 — Occupation × economic period

We test whether occupational differences change across 2004–2008, 2009–2014, 2015–2019 and 2020–2024. The model includes occupation, economic period and their interaction. A joint Wald test assesses whether all 24 interaction coefficients are zero. Managers and 2004–2008 are the reference categories.

Code 
rq13_data = analysis_sample[["IDPERS", "YEAR", "OCCUPATION", "JOB_SATISFACTION"]].dropna().copy()
rq13_data = rq13_data[rq13_data["OCCUPATION"].isin(range(1, 10))].copy()
rq13_data["OCCUPATION"] = rq13_data["OCCUPATION"].astype(int)
rq13_data["ECONOMIC_PERIOD"] = pd.cut(
    rq13_data["YEAR"], bins=[2003, 2008, 2014, 2019, 2024],
    labels=["2004–2008", "2009–2014", "2015–2019", "2020–2024"]
)
model_rq13 = smf.ols(
    "JOB_SATISFACTION ~ C(OCCUPATION) * C(ECONOMIC_PERIOD)", data=rq13_data
).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": rq13_data["IDPERS"]})
interaction_terms = [t for t in model_rq13.params.index if ":" in t]
interaction_test = model_rq13.wald_test(" = 0, ".join(interaction_terms) + " = 0", scalar=True)
selected_interactions = {2: "Professionals", 3: "Technicians", 5: "Service and sales"}
interaction_rows = []
for code, name in selected_interactions.items():
    term = next(t for t in interaction_terms if f"[T.{code}]" in t and "[T.2020–2024]" in t)
    interaction_rows.append({"Occupation": name, "Interaction (points)": model_rq13.params[term], "p-value": model_rq13.pvalues[term]})
display(pd.DataFrame(interaction_rows).round(4))
print(f"N = {len(rq13_data):,}; respondents = {rq13_data['IDPERS'].nunique():,}; Wald chi-square({len(interaction_terms)}) = {float(interaction_test.statistic):.2f}; p = {float(interaction_test.pvalue):.4f}; R² = {model_rq13.rsquared:.3f}")
N = 124,635; respondents = 22,242; Wald chi-square(24) = 45.88; p = 0.0046; R² = 0.009

As shown in Table 6, the joint interaction is statistically significant (χ²(24) = 45.88, p = 0.0046; 124,635 observations, R² = 0.009). Thus, occupational gaps are not completely stable across periods. In 2020–2024, the gap relative to managers is lower than in 2004–2008 for professionals (−0.190), technicians (−0.161) and service and sales workers (−0.174). These are changes in relative occupational gaps, not absolute changes in those groups’ satisfaction. Individual interaction p-values should be interpreted cautiously because many comparisons were tested.

5 Findings and Discussion

Taken together, the results in Table 4, Table 5 and Table 6 support three preliminary conclusions. First, occupational, demographic, regional and employment-arrangement differences are detectable, but the adjusted model explains only a small fraction of individual satisfaction variation. Second, the three event windows show different patterns, including a small temporary rise in 2020 rather than a uniform decline during crises. Third, occupational differences vary across broader economic periods, particularly in comparisons with managers in 2020–2024.

For management, these findings suggest that employee satisfaction is not uniform across worker groups or periods. However, the observed differences are generally modest and should not be treated as a basis for causal claims or direct policy prescriptions. Limitations include unweighted regressions, changing sample composition, unobserved characteristics, multiple hypothesis tests, bounded satisfaction scores, and incomplete incorporation of the survey’s complex design. Further robustness work could assess weighted models, alternative event windows and within-person changes. The Conclusion section summarises progress and next steps for the final report.

6 Conclusion

6.1 Summary

This project examines how job satisfaction in Switzerland differs across occupational and demographic groups, how it changes around major economic events, and whether occupational differences remain stable over time. We use the Swiss Household Panel (SHP) for 2004–2024. After combining and cleaning annual respondent records, the full dataset contains 305,462 respondent-year observations from 45,632 individuals. Our employed sample contains 124,769 observations from 22,265 individuals; the main analysis sample has 124,766 observations after excluding missing age or sex information. We explored distributions and trends, compared group averages, and estimated ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions with standard errors clustered by respondent to account for repeated observations. The regressions are unweighted, while a separate descriptive check uses available SHP survey weights.

Five findings stand out. First, average reported job satisfaction fell from 8.212 in 2004 to 7.815 in 2024 on the 0–10 scale (unweighted), with a similar but somewhat larger decline in the survey-weighted check (8.207 to 7.711). Second, occupational differences are statistically detectable: in the year-adjusted model, agricultural workers score 0.560 points, managers 0.317 points, and professionals 0.231 points above clerical support workers on average. Third, occupation, age group, sex, region of residence and employment arrangement are jointly significant in the adjusted model, although its R² of 0.039 shows that these variables explain only a small share of individual variation. Fourth, the event-window comparisons are not uniform: satisfaction is slightly lower around 2015, while 2020 shows a small temporary increase relative to 2019; the 2009 event-year difference is not statistically significant. Fifth, occupational gaps change across the four broader economic periods (joint interaction χ²(24) = 45.88, p = 0.0046), suggesting that differences between occupations are not completely stable. Together, these findings answer our research questions at a preliminary, descriptive level: worker characteristics and historical periods are associated with job satisfaction, but the models do not establish why these differences arise or whether economic events caused them.

6.2 Limitations

The SHP provides a large longitudinal dataset, but coverage and missingness affect comparability. We restricted the project to 2004–2024 because general job satisfaction was unavailable for 2000–2003. The employed sample excludes records without usable occupation or job-satisfaction values, and the adjusted regression uses only 104,526 observations from 18,363 respondents because additional covariates must also be observed. If excluded respondents differ systematically from those retained, the reported averages and group comparisons may be biased. Sample composition can also change between waves, so changes in annual means do not necessarily represent changes experienced by the same individuals. The REGION variable measures region of residence, not the location of employment.

There are also measurement and modelling limitations. Job satisfaction is a self-reported, bounded 0–10 score; treating it as a continuous outcome in OLS makes differences easy to interpret but does not fully represent its discrete distribution or possible ceiling effects. Respondent-clustered standard errors address correlation between repeated observations from the same person, but they do not control for all unobserved personal or job characteristics. The regressions do not fully incorporate the SHP’s complex survey design. Although 121,547 of 124,769 employed-sample observations have positive cross-sectional survey weights, the weighted trend was only a descriptive sensitivity check, not a weighted replication of every model. We have not completed comprehensive model diagnostics or sensitivity checks. In addition, the short before/during/after event windows capture associations between survey years, not causal effects of the 2009 crisis, the 2015 Swiss franc shock or COVID-19. Testing multiple groups and interactions also increases the chance of isolated significant results. Consequently, conclusions should be limited to the analysed SHP respondents and should not automatically be generalised to all Swiss workers or to other countries.

6.3 Future Work

Before the final submission, we will prioritise the following feasible improvements:

  1. Check data definitions and sample composition. Confirm variable labels and coding against the SHP documentation, especially sex, occupation and employment-arrangement categories. Report missingness by year and compare the characteristics of retained and excluded observations to assess possible selection bias.
  2. Strengthen survey-weight robustness checks. Repeat the main occupation and year comparisons using the available cross-sectional weights, then compare coefficient directions and magnitudes with the unweighted estimates. Document which weights are appropriate for each analysis and acknowledge any remaining survey-design limitations.
  3. Check model diagnostics and sensitivity. Inspect residual patterns and the distribution of fitted values, and assess whether the main results remain similar under alternative specifications or age groupings. Because satisfaction is bounded and discrete, consider an ordinal model as a sensitivity check if time and course scope allow.
  4. Make better use of the panel structure. Where respondent IDs are consistent across waves, compare changes within the same individuals, for example using a respondent fixed-effects model. This would reduce bias from stable unobserved differences between people, although it would still not establish causation.
  5. Test the stability of event and occupation findings. Compare alternative event windows (for example, two years before and after each event), examine occupation-specific trends with sufficient observations, and distinguish robust patterns from isolated significant coefficients. We will keep the interpretation focused on associations rather than attributing changes directly to the events.

These steps build on the data preparation, EDA and preliminary models already completed. The main priority is validating the existing results and clarifying their limitations, rather than adding unrelated analyses. This will help us produce a more reliable final assessment of how job satisfaction varies across Swiss workers and over time.
